content.text: Three weeks after the oath, Falanaras learned that stolen Light punished hesitation more readily than zeal.

Daric’s practice blade struck his guard and drove him half a step across the training court. Falanaras let the impact travel through both hands, turned his new two-handed sword along the pressure, and called the bond open. Red-gold radiance ran down the fuller. He cut upward before Daric could recover.

Daric caught the blow on a shield of Light. The collision filled the old Farstrider court with a crack like splitting timber. Radiance sprayed between them, bright enough to stain the surrounding arches crimson-gold, and both men broke apart before the pressure could become a contest of appetite.
“Late,” Liadrin said.

Falanaras lowered the sword. Its longer hilt still felt unfamiliar after years with a spellbreaker’s glaive. The weapon had been issued with the black-and-crimson plate now enclosing his shoulders and chest, both chosen to separate the new order from Silvermoon’s gold-bright ranks. The colors made every mistake conspicuous.
“The shield held,” he said.

“Daric’s did. Yours remained in M’uru until the moment had nearly passed.” Liadrin stood at the court’s edge with her ranseur grounded beside one boot. Fine gold still showed beneath the green of her eyes. “Again. Decide before the blow arrives.”

Falanaras reset his stance. Beyond Daric, Theron trained with two other knights beneath the broken shade of an ornamental arch. He carried a broad shield and a single-handed sword, trusting weight and patience where Falanaras had been taught to seize the enemy’s working and split it open. Light curved around Theron’s shield whenever a strike threatened the soldier behind him.

The Blood Knights had discovered their differences quickly. Daric broke pressure wherever it gathered. Althene used the Light with the same restraint she had once brought to arrows and field dressings. Theron built shelter. Falanaras saw currents: the red-gold bond below his own pulse, the ordinary magic in the training wards, the momentary charge Daric drew from a practice seal before striking.

They still Mana Tapped as every sin’dorei soldier had learned to do. During drills, they stripped force from warded weapons, took measured threads from hostile exercises, and spent that power on movement or defense. The bond to M’uru had added another weapon. It had not made the old one shameful.

Daric attacked again. This time Falanaras opened the bond as the veteran’s shoulder turned. Light reached him with a pressure beneath the breastbone and the remembered echo of a distant cry. He drove the thought aside without denying it. His sword met Daric’s practice blade in a burst of radiance, slid past, and stopped against the edge of Daric’s gorget.
Daric glanced down. “I preferred the glaive.”
“You preferred knowing where the blade would be.”
“That was most of the appeal.”
Liadrin crossed the court. “Better. You heard the source and acted anyway.”
“I always hear it.”
“Good.” Her answer held no gentleness. “Forgetting would make you dangerous.”
Across the court, one of the younger knights knelt beside a ranger with a practice cut along his forearm. Light poured over the wound in an extravagant wash. The ranger hissed and tried to pull away.
Althene caught the healer’s wrist. “Enough to close it,” she said. “Enough to return him to the line. You are treating a cut, not attempting to make him luminous.”
From the gallery wall, Lethira called, “Let him continue. I’ve always wanted a target visible from the Ghostlands.”
Theron looked toward her without lowering his shield. “You came to observe?”
“I came to confirm that black plate has not improved either of you.” Lethira’s bow rested across her knees. She had kept her ranger leathers and crimson cloak, as promised. “The result is mixed.”

The western gate opened before Theron could answer. Two Farstriders entered at speed, followed by a dark ranger in weather-stained black. The training court quieted by degrees. Bows lowered. Practice wards dimmed. Falanaras recognized Serenya Duskrunner before she pulled back her hood.

She had changed little since the ruined way station. Undeath preserved some faces with cruel precision. Her skin remained ash-pale, her eyes a cold red, and the black-fletched arrows at her shoulder might have belonged to the ranger Lethira had once known if the hands beneath them had carried warmth.
Lethira was already on her feet.
Serenya’s gaze touched her and moved on. “Lady Liadrin. Captain Dawnspear. Tranquillien will be under attack before nightfall.”

Ranger-General Halduron arrived while Serenya was pinning a mud-stained map to the practice table. He brought no honor guard, only three officers and the expression of a man already spending soldiers he did not possess.

“Amani raiders crossed west from the Zul’Aman approaches at dawn,” Serenya said. Her finger followed a broken line through the eastern Ghostlands. “They struck two Scourge camps, burned the controlling fetishes, and drove what rose toward the road. They are herding the undead with fire, noise, and fresh bodies.”
One of Halduron’s officers swore under his breath.
“Numbers?” Halduron asked.

“Sixty that walked when we saw them. More answered the disturbance behind us. Ghouls, skeletons, two necromancers, at least one abomination. The Amani have stayed outside bow range. They do not need to take Tranquillien themselves if they can bury it under the Scourge.”

Falanaras studied the map. Tranquillien sat where the northern road narrowed between ruined estates and the Dead Scar’s western wound. The outpost had walls in the charitable sense: sections of old stone, timber palisades, and enough repaired roofs to shelter a garrison. If it fell, the road into restored Eversong would lie open to every remnant stirred behind the first surge.
“My scouts marked the herd’s eastern edge,” Serenya continued. “Then the trolls cut the trail behind us. Four of mine remain south of the outpost. I came north with the warning.”
Lethira’s voice flattened. “You left four.”
“I made the only choice that delivered the warning.” Serenya did not look at her. “They knew the risk.”

Halduron placed two fingers east of Serenya’s route. “The raiders are the hand. The Scourge are the weapon. I’ll take the Farstrider companies after the hand before it circles north and repeats the trick.” He looked to Liadrin. “Can your order hold the road?”

The question settled over the black-and-crimson figures around the table. Three weeks of wards, measured cuts, controlled exhaustion, and Liadrin’s unyielding corrections. None of it had included an enemy trying to tear the current from their hands before they could govern it.
“Yes,” Liadrin said.
Halduron’s eyes moved across the candidates who had become knights. “That was not ceremony.”

“Neither was my answer.” Liadrin turned to Falanaras. “You will lead the strike file. Daric with you. Theron commands the shield file. Althene oversees field recovery and anyone who mistakes abundance for skill.”
Althene inclined her head. “A broad jurisdiction.”
“Exercise it.” Liadrin looked to Lethira. “Your rangers know the ground.”
Lethira’s attention remained on Serenya. “We’ll guide you south.”
“You will guide the Blood Knights,” Halduron corrected. “Duskrunner returns to her scouts if she can reach them. You will not abandon Tranquillien to settle an old wound.”
Lethira met his gaze. “Understood.”

They left within the quarter hour. There was no time to polish the new armor or decide whether the people lining the southern road saw saviors, blasphemers, or another expensive promise from the city. Falanaras saw a woman draw her child closer at the sight of Liadrin’s red-gold eyes. Farther on, an old veteran raised two fingers in salute.

The Blood Knights rode at the center, fourteen black-and-crimson figures among Lethira’s ranger file. Their armor made them look like an order with decades behind it. Their silence betrayed how recently each had learned the others’ fighting habits.
Theron brought his horse alongside Falanaras. “First field deployment.”
“You noticed.”
“The absence of padded weapons was persuasive.” Theron adjusted the shield lashed behind his saddle. “Do you think it works the same against the Scourge?”

Falanaras remembered M’uru’s chamber, the holy pressure that had quieted every ache in his body. He remembered Edric at the ruined way station, gold blazing against rotted flesh. “No,” he said. “I think it works better.”

By the time they crossed into the Ghostlands, the air had changed. Eversong’s autumn warmth thinned into damp cold. Dead trunks crowded the road, their bark gray beneath creeping rot. The Dead Scar lay east as a strip of poisoned earth where the horizon seemed bruised.

The first evidence of the Amani appeared at a crossroads: a Scourge fetish split by a stone-headed axe, troll footprints leading east, and three corpses stripped of their controlling runes. Someone had smeared pitch across the dead grass and set it alight to force the risen bodies westward.
Lethira crouched beside the tracks. Serenya stood opposite her, equally still.
“Six raiders,” Lethira said. “One heavy. They doubled back.”
“Eight,” Serenya said. “Two walked in the burned ground.”
Lethira’s jaw tightened. She found the softened prints beneath the ash and rose without argument. “Eight. East toward Halduron.”
It was the first judgment of Serenya’s that she had accepted since the dark ranger’s death. No one acknowledged it. Falanaras suspected that was the only reason the moment survived.
A horn sounded ahead: one long note, two short. Tranquillien’s alarm.
Liadrin lifted her ranseur. “Ride.”

Tranquillien came into view through smoke and bare branches. Its northern watchtower leaned above a low ring of broken walls. Fresh timber filled old breaches, pale against scorched stone. A dozen defenders held the southern approach while laborers dragged supply carts into a courtyard that had lost half its roof.
Beyond them, the Ghostlands moved.

Ghouls ran between the trees in crooked bursts. Skeletons crowded behind them, armor and bones gathered from several wars. Farther back, two necromancers drove the surge with hooked staves while an abomination lumbered through the smoke, its stitched shoulders brushing dead branches aside.

The outpost commander met Liadrin at the gate. Blood darkened one sleeve. “We have twenty-three who can hold a weapon. Seven more wounded. The southern palisade will take one rush if the abomination reaches it.”

“It will not,” Liadrin said. “Lethira, towers and flanks. Theron, shield file across the gate. Falanaras, we break the first rush beyond the wall. Keep them far enough out that Althene has room to work.”
Serenya pointed southeast. “My scouts will be along that drainage cut if they still have ground. I can reach them from the lower wall.”
Lethira studied the cut, then the advancing undead. “Two rangers with you. No more.”
Serenya nodded once. The agreement carried no forgiveness. It carried coordinates, numbers, and a route likely to keep three people from being surrounded. On a battlefield, that was enough to matter.

Falanaras dismounted and drew his sword. The bond stirred before he called it, M’uru’s Light alert beneath his pulse. Around him, the strike file formed with Daric on his right. Their black plate seemed to drink the color from the Ghostlands until red-gold lines kindled along gauntlets and blades.
“We have practiced this,” Daric said.
The first ghouls cleared the trees. Falanaras heard their claws tearing the road.
“Not this,” he said.
Liadrin’s ranseur came down. “Advance.”
The Blood Knights met the Scourge twenty paces beyond the wall.

Falanaras cut through the first ghoul’s shoulder. Light entered the corpse with the blade and burst outward through its ribs. The creature came apart in ash, bone, and a flash so bright the next two recoiled. Daric struck into that hesitation, his heavy sword trailing fire. Three skeletons collapsed before the edge reached them.

The effect was more violent than any practice target had suggested. Holy power did not merely damage the undead. It rejected the magic holding them together. Falanaras felt necromantic bindings flare across his spellbreaker senses, exposed and suddenly fragile beneath the stolen radiance.
“Left anchor,” he called.

The knights turned with him. Rangers on the wall loosed into the gap, each arrow choosing a rune-bright skull or joint. One ranger caught the current from an incoming death bolt, pulled a measured thread through her bow hand, and spent it on the enchantment carrying her next arrow. The shot crossed the field in a violet streak and shattered a necromancer’s ward.

Falanaras reached for the failing spell with every sin’dorei instinct sharpened by spellbreaker training. He stripped enough power to collapse its outer weave, stopped before the corrupted current could flood him, and drove his sword through the exposed center. Light followed. Six skeletons fell at once.
The hunger within him quieted under M’uru’s bond. The stolen necromancy still left a bitter trace on his tongue. Both facts entered his judgment. Neither required shame.

A ghoul slipped beneath Daric’s guard and opened the seam below his arm. Althene appeared before he had fully turned. She pressed one hand to the wound, gave it a narrow pulse of Light, and shoved him back toward the line.
“Closed,” she said. “Pain means you remain informed.”
Daric returned to the fighting without complaint.
The first rush broke before it reached Theron’s file. For three breaths, Falanaras believed they had misjudged the threat.
Then the abomination charged.

It came through its own lesser troops, crushing bones under slabbed feet. Iron hooks swung from chains stitched into its arms. The remaining necromancer poured power into the thing from behind, thickening every binding until Falanaras saw a web of diseased blue-white light drawn tight through dead flesh.
“Back to the shields!” Liadrin ordered.
The strike file yielded in pairs. The abomination’s hook tore the ground where Falanaras had stood. He retreated through Theron’s line as curved shields of Light locked together across the gate.
The creature hit them.

Red-gold radiance bowed inward. Theron dropped to one knee behind his physical shield, teeth bared, while the two knights beside him lost their footing. The palisade groaned. Falanaras felt the impact travel through every linked current and descend toward the captive source beneath Silvermoon.
One of the shield knights reached for more. The bond widened around him, hungry in a way Light should never have felt.
Liadrin struck the back of his breastplate with her gauntlet. “Hold what you chose. Do not gorge because fear gave you permission.”

The knight choked the current down. Theron shifted his stance and took the missing weight through his own shield. “Falanaras,” he said, each syllable compressed beneath the pressure. “Useful time for your specialty.”

Falanaras set both hands on his sword and looked through the abomination’s flesh to the bindings beneath. The necromancer had layered them crudely because abundance made elegance unnecessary. Every layer returned to three knots along the spine.
“Daric. With me.”

Theron opened a gap. Falanaras and Daric passed through under the creature’s raised hook. Daric struck the knee with enough Light to burst rotted tissue from the joint. Falanaras caught the necromantic reinforcement as it surged toward the wound, drained the leading edge, and redirected the rest through his blade.
The sword entered the first knot. Holy fire raced along the binding web.

The abomination screamed through three throats. Daric broke the second knot. Liadrin’s ranseur descended on the third with a column of red-gold light that split the corpse from shoulder to hip. The creature collapsed before the palisade in a steaming ruin.
A ragged cheer rose from the defenders. It died when horns answered from the trees and another mass of undead emerged behind the first.
At the lower wall, a black-fletched arrow struck the parapet beside Lethira. A strip of gray cloth had been tied beneath the head.
Lethira read the signal and looked toward Serenya. “Your scouts?”

“Alive. Cut off in the drainage cut.” Serenya listened to something only trained ears or death could detect. “They have the necromancer’s flank. If we draw them north, my people can break the control line.”
Lethira studied the approaching wave. “That exposes the eastern wall.”
“For twenty breaths.”

Old grief crossed Lethira’s face and vanished beneath calculation. She counted the road, the wall, the black-fletched arrow, and the undead advancing between them. “Falanaras,” she called. “Can your people give the lower cut twenty breaths?”
Liadrin answered before he could. “His file can. Theron holds the gate.”
Theron reset his shield among the bodies. “I had hoped to become decorative after the first wave.”
Falanaras gathered Daric and four knights. “Lower wall. We cover the Forsaken withdrawal.”
One knight hesitated. “They are already dead.”
Falanaras looked at Serenya, at the face Lethira had once known alive, and then at the outpost whose defenders could not survive another full assault. “They are holding our enemy’s flank. Move.”

The lower gate opened onto a slope choked with thornbrush and collapsed stone. Falanaras led the strike file through while rangers above shifted their fire north. The new undead wave bent after the movement, drawn toward the apparent weakness exactly as Serenya had predicted.

The drainage cut lay thirty paces away. Four dark figures fought back-to-back within it, black arrows spent, curved blades rising and falling among ghouls. One Forsaken had lost an arm. Another carried a spear through his ribs and continued fighting around it.
Serenya gave a shrill whistle. Her scouts turned toward the sound without surprise.
“Now,” Falanaras said.

The Blood Knights planted their weapons. Falanaras opened the bond and felt the others answer through Liadrin’s deeper link. Light gathered between them, rough at the edges because they had never built a field ward over broken ground or beneath a rain of death bolts.

The first bolt struck before the ward had fully formed. Daric Mana Tapped its outer charge, taking enough to blunt the impact, and the half-built shield caught the rest. Red-gold light spread across the slope from stone to dead tree, leaving a narrow passage between the Forsaken and Tranquillien.

Pain drove through Falanaras’s arms. The ward carried every strike into the bond. Behind its brilliance he felt M’uru’s captivity as a pressure without distance, a living source forced to answer soldiers it had never chosen.
The shield held.

Serenya’s scouts withdrew through the passage in disciplined order. The one-armed dark ranger dragged a wounded blood elf from the thornbrush as he passed, hooking his remaining hand through the ranger’s harness. Another Forsaken paused beneath the ward long enough to fire a recovered arrow into the necromancer directing the flank.
The arrow struck the necromancer’s shoulder. Lethira’s shot followed from the wall and pierced its throat.
Control vanished from the eastern wave. Ghouls stumbled into one another. Skeletons turned toward the last command they had heard and exposed their flank to the outpost’s archers.
“Drop the ward,” Falanaras ordered. “Strike.”

They released together. The protection collapsed inward and ran along six weapons. Falanaras charged through the dying radiance. His sword sheared a ghoul in half, then rose through the ribs of a skeleton as Daric’s heavier blows broke the line beside him.

Forsaken arrows passed over their shoulders. The dark rangers had reached the lower wall and turned immediately, firing into the exposed Scourge flank. Their black shafts found controlling runes and old wounds. Blood elf arrows joined them, brighter with enchantment, until the air between wall and trees seemed stitched with two kinds of precision.

At the main gate, Theron’s shields advanced. He and his file pushed behind overlapping curves of Light, sheltering wounded defenders as Althene moved among them. She sealed an opened belly, stopped a ranger’s bleeding, and sent both living soldiers toward the rear before spending any more power than survival required.

A death bolt struck Theron’s shield and spread across it in black veins. He reached through the impact, drained a measured share of the hostile spell, and fed the stolen charge into the muscles bracing his arm. The corruption dimmed. His red-gold ward endured.

The sight would have been impossible once: a blood elf shield wall carrying coerced Holy Light while undead rangers killed the Scourge from a broken Thalassian outpost. Falanaras had no breath to decide what it meant. A ghoul lunged, and he answered with steel.

The remaining necromancer tried to retreat. Serenya appeared on the slope below it and drove both blades beneath its ribs. When it folded, she tore the control focus from its belt and threw it toward Falanaras.

He caught the focus in one gauntlet. The thing writhed with commands, bindings, and enough concentrated necromancy to make his senses ache. Every sin’dorei instinct urged him to take the useful portion before destroying it.

He did. One bounded draw exposed the command structure and gave his exhausted body the strength for another strike. He stopped with power still churning inside the focus, set it on a stone, and brought the red-gold edge of his sword down through its center.

The focus shattered. Across the field, the last organized ranks of the Scourge collapsed into isolated creatures. Rangers marked them. Blood Knights finished them. The outpost defenders drove the survivors away from the road until the trees swallowed the final shrieks.
Silence arrived unevenly. A bowstring snapped once after there was no target. Someone called for a healer. One of the Forsaken laughed without humor while pulling the spear from his ribs.

Falanaras lowered his sword. Light still ran along the blade, eager and effective. He closed the bond to a narrower current. Far beneath Silvermoon, M’uru remained chained. Around him, living soldiers remained alive.

By dusk, Tranquillien smelled of lamp oil, wet ash, and the bitter compounds Althene used to clean wounds after the Light had closed them. The order’s healing had saved six soldiers who would likely have died before a conventional field priest reached them. It had not saved everyone.

Three blood elves lay beneath ranger cloaks near the northern wall. One Blood Knight sat beside them with a broken hand wrapped against his chest, staring at the bodies as though the power inside him had promised omnipotence and betrayed the claim. Liadrin knelt, spoke to him too quietly for Falanaras to hear, and left him with grief rather than correction.
Theron found Falanaras near the ruined gate. His shield was split along the lower rim. “Useful,” he said.

The word carried the same weight it had when Theron first considered what M’uru’s power could become. Falanaras looked over the courtyard: wounded rangers breathing because stolen Light had closed their wounds, defenders stacking Scourge remains for burning, black-armored knights moving with the stunned care of soldiers who had learned exactly what their training could do.
“Very,” he said.

A horn sounded from the eastern road after sunset. Halduron’s Farstriders returned in scattered groups, carrying two prisoners and enough bloodied Amani weapons to prove the raiders had paid for their design. The trolls had withdrawn toward Zul’Aman. Halduron listened to Liadrin’s report beside the gate, then examined the field in silence.
“You held,” he said at last.
Liadrin rested both hands on her ranseur. Fatigue had deepened the gold under her eyes. “We were useful.”
“So was the company you kept.” Halduron glanced toward the Forsaken assembling beneath the lower tower. “I will decide what to call that after we have secured the road.”

The decision began before anyone named it. Blood elf sentries took the northern wall. Forsaken scouts claimed the lower tower, where they could watch the southern approaches without passing through the living quarters. Supply carts were unloaded into a shared storehouse under two locks, one key held by each force. Tranquillien became a foothold through guard rosters and repaired timber rather than declarations.

Lethira stood beside the drainage cut while Serenya checked the fletching on a recovered arrow. The living ranger had blood on one cheek. The dark ranger had stitched a tear in her side with black cord and apparently considered the matter settled.
“Eight raiders,” Lethira said.
Serenya looked at her. “Eight.”
“Your flank held.”
“Your shield reached us.” Serenya’s dead face gave little away. “We kept one another from becoming useful to the Scourge.”
Lethira’s mouth tightened at the phrasing. “Do not make me regret agreeing with you.”
“I remember that threat from when it had fewer qualifications.”
For one instant, Lethira looked stricken. Then she turned toward the outpost. “Take the southern watch. My people need sleep.”
Serenya inclined her head and went to issue the order.

Falanaras watched from the wall. The alliance between them was too large a word for what had happened. Trust was scarcely better. A field judgment had been accepted. A withdrawal had been covered. Wounded soldiers had been pulled clear by hands that no longer lived. The road remained open because each force had done what the other could not.

Below him, the Blood Knights gathered their wounded beneath black-and-crimson cloaks. Their first battle had given Liadrin proof stronger than any controlled chamber could offer. They could shatter the undead, protect a failing line, and close wounds fast enough to return soldiers to the defense. Quel’Thalas would use them again.
Pride came without reluctance. The lives below deserved it. The road deserved it. The outpost standing against the dark deserved it.

M’uru’s suffering remained true beneath that pride. Falanaras did not offer the victory as payment for the captive’s pain or pretend usefulness had purified the means. He carried both facts because surrendering either would make the other easier to abuse.

South of Tranquillien, Forsaken eyes watched the road. North of it, sin’dorei sentries held the way home. Between them, new timber rose against old ruins while the bodies of the Scourge burned beyond the wall.
For the first time since Arthas had cut the Dead Scar through Quel’Thalas, Tranquillien’s ruined ground was being reclaimed by sin’dorei and Forsaken hands together.
